questions.title: Question 1: Calls and returns (12 marks)
questions.prompt: A recursive method `power(x, y)` returns 1 when `y == 0` and `x * power(x, y - 1)` otherwise. Trace `power(2, 4)`. Show (a) every parameter value while the calls descend, (b) what each call is waiting to multiply, and (c) every expression and result while the returns unwind. State the answer and the number of calls. (12 marks)

steps.title: Read the question
steps.body: The command word is 'trace', so the answer is a table with the calls going down and the results coming back up. `x` stays 2 and `y` goes 4, 3, 2, 1, 0.

steps.title: Plan
steps.body: Write one row per call. Fill the Returned column going down (the expression with the recursive call unevaluated) and the Result column from the bottom up.

steps.title: Solution
steps.body: Going down: `power(2, 4)` waits for `2 * power(2, 3)`; `power(2, 3)` waits for `2 * power(2, 2)`; `power(2, 2)` waits for `2 * power(2, 1)`; `power(2, 1)` waits for `2 * power(2, 0)`; `power(2, 0)` is the base case and returns 1. Coming back: `power(2, 1)` = 2 * 1 = 2; `power(2, 2)` = 2 * 2 = 4; `power(2, 3)` = 2 * 4 = 8; `power(2, 4)` = 2 * 8 = 16.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: 2 to the 4 is 16. The calls are for `y` = 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0, so there are 5 calls: `y + 1`.

questions.answer: **Final answer.** `power(2, 4)` returns **16**, using **5 calls**. Marks: 4 for the descending calls, 4 for the waiting expressions, 4 for the unwinding results.

questions.title: Question 2: Diagnose termination (12 marks)
questions.prompt: For each method, identify the base case, the changing input, and whether the input gets closer to the base case. Say what happens for the input given and repair any method that does not terminate. (a) `static int a(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return n + a(n + 1); }` called as `a(3)`. (b) `static int b(int n) { if (n == 1) return 1; return n + b(n - 2); }` called as `b(4)` and `b(5)`. (c) `static int c(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return c(n - 1) + c(n - 2); }` called as `c(1)`. (12 marks)

steps.title: Method (a)
steps.body: Base case `n == 0`. The input goes 3, 4, 5, ... so it moves away from 0 and `a(3)` ends in a `StackOverflowError`. Repair: call `a(n - 1)`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Method (b)
steps.body: Base case `n == 1`. The input goes down by 2. From 5 it goes 5, 3, 1 and stops, giving 9. From 4 it goes 4, 2, 0, -2 and steps over 1, so `b(4)` ends in a `StackOverflowError`. Repair: use a range as the base case, `if (n <= 1)`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Method (c)
steps.body: Base case `n == 0` only. `c(1)` calls `c(0)` and `c(-1)`; `c(-1)` calls `c(-2)` and `c(-3)`, which go further below the base case, so it ends in a `StackOverflowError`. A method that calls itself with `n - 2` needs a second base case for 1. Repair: add `if (n == 1) return 1;`. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Rule.** Every call must move towards a base case that it cannot step over, and a method that reaches back by two positions needs two base cases.

questions.title: Question 3: Recursive array sum (14 marks)
questions.prompt: Write `static int sum(int[] data, int index)`. The method must return 0 when `index == data.length`. Trace it on `[4, 7, 2]`, then state the time and the auxiliary space used. (14 marks)

steps.title: Read the question
steps.body: The base case is given. The method adds `data[index]` to the sum of the rest, so the recursive call uses `index + 1`.

steps.title: Solution
steps.body: `static int sum(int[] data, int index) { if (index == data.length) { return 0; } return data[index] + sum(data, index + 1); }`. (5 marks)

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: `sum(data, 0)` waits for `4 + sum(data, 1)`; `sum(data, 1)` waits for `7 + sum(data, 2)`; `sum(data, 2)` waits for `2 + sum(data, 3)`; `sum(data, 3)` is the base case and returns 0. Unwinding: 2 + 0 = 2, then 7 + 2 = 9, then 4 + 9 = 13. (5 marks)

steps.title: Cost
steps.body: One call per element plus the base case, so the time is O(n). Every call is waiting at once, so there are n + 1 stack frames and the auxiliary space is O(n). Java does not remove the frames. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** `sum(data, 0)` returns **13**; time O(n), auxiliary space O(n).

questions.title: Question 4: Recursive search (12 marks)
questions.prompt: Write a recursive method `indexOf(int[] a, int target, int i)` that returns the index of the first occurrence of `target` at or after position `i`, or -1. Trace it on `{10, 20, 30, 20}` for the targets 30 and 99, writing the base-case condition with its values at every call. (12 marks)

steps.title: Plan
steps.body: Two base cases: `i == a.length` (not found, return -1) and `a[i] == target` (found, return `i`). Otherwise search from `i + 1`.

steps.title: Solution
steps.body: `static int indexOf(int[] a, int target, int i) { if (i == a.length) { return -1; } if (a[i] == target) { return i; } return indexOf(a, target, i + 1); }`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Trace for 30
steps.body: `i = 0`: `0 == 4` false, `10 == 30` false. `i = 1`: `1 == 4` false, `20 == 30` false. `i = 2`: `2 == 4` false, `30 == 30` true, return 2. Three calls. (4 marks)

steps.title: Trace for 99
steps.body: `i = 0, 1, 2, 3`: the element is never 99. `i = 4`: `4 == 4` true, return -1. Five calls, and the -1 passes back up unchanged. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** Target 30 gives index **2** after 3 calls; target 99 gives **-1** after 5 calls.

questions.title: Question 5: String recursion (10 marks)
questions.prompt: (a) Write a recursive method `String reverse(String s)`. (b) Write a recursive method `boolean isPalindrome(String s)` that drops both ends on each call, and say which string lengths its base case must handle and why. (c) A student writes `return s.charAt(0) + s.charAt(0) + doubled(s.substring(1));` to double every character. Say what `doubled("abc")` returns. (10 marks)

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: `static String reverse(String s) { if (s.isEmpty()) { return ""; } return reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0); }`. The first character is attached after the call returns, so it ends up last. (3 marks)

steps.title: Part (b)
steps.body: `static boolean isPalindrome(String s) { if (s.length() <= 1) { return true; } if (s.charAt(0) != s.charAt(s.length() - 1)) { return false; } return isPalindrome(s.substring(1, s.length() - 1)); }`. The base case must accept lengths 0 and 1: an even-length string shrinks to 0 and an odd-length string shrinks to 1. With only length 0, `"aba"` reaches `"b"` and then `substring(1, 0)` throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Part (c)
steps.body: `s.charAt(0) + s.charAt(0)` adds two `char` values as numbers (97 + 97 = 194). `doubled("abc")` returns `"194196198"`. Repair: start the expression with a `String`, `"" + c + c + doubled(...)`. (3 marks)

questions.title: Question 6: Recursive binary search (12 marks)
questions.prompt: The array `{8, 18, 23, 29, 34}` is sorted. Write a recursive binary search `search(int[] a, int key, int lo, int hi)` and trace it for the keys 29 and 5, showing `lo`, `hi`, `mid` and `a[mid]` in each call and the number of calls. (12 marks)

steps.title: Solution
steps.body: `static int search(int[] a, int key, int lo, int hi) { if (lo > hi) { return -1; } int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if (a[mid] == key) { return mid; } if (a[mid] < key) { return search(a, key, mid + 1, hi); } return search(a, key, lo, mid - 1); }`. Both new ranges exclude `mid`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Key 29
steps.body: Call 1: `lo = 0`, `hi = 4`, `mid = 2`, `a[2] = 23`, smaller than 29, so go right. Call 2: `lo = 3`, `hi = 4`, `mid = 3`, `a[3] = 29`, found, return 3. Two calls. (4 marks)

steps.title: Key 5
steps.body: Call 1: `lo = 0`, `hi = 4`, `mid = 2`, `a[2] = 23`, larger than 5, so go left. Call 2: `lo = 0`, `hi = 1`, `mid = 0`, `a[0] = 8`, larger than 5, so go left. Call 3: `lo = 0`, `hi = -1`, `lo > hi`, return -1. Three calls. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** Key 29 returns **3** after 2 calls; key 5 returns **-1** after 3 calls.

questions.title: Question 7: Recursion against iteration (12 marks)
questions.prompt: Write recursive and iterative methods for the factorial of a non-negative `int`. Compare their output, time, auxiliary space, readability and handling of invalid input. Do not claim that Java removes tail calls. (12 marks)

steps.title: The methods
steps.body: Recursive: `static long fact(int n) { if (n <= 1) { return 1; } return n * fact(n - 1); }`. Iterative: `static long factLoop(int n) { long result = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) { result *= i; } return result; }`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body: Output: the same for every `n` from 0 up. Time: O(n) for both. Auxiliary space: the recursion keeps `n` frames on the stack, O(n); the loop uses a few variables, O(1). Readability: the recursion mirrors the definition. Invalid input: a negative `n` returns 1 from both as written, so state a precondition or throw an `IllegalArgumentException`. (6 marks)

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: Both overflow a `long` at 21, giving a negative number without warning. Java does not turn the recursion into a loop, so a very large `n` also risks `StackOverflowError` for the recursive version only. (2 marks)

questions.answer: **Rule.** Same result and time, different space: the recursion costs a stack frame per call.

questions.title: Question 8: Convert a loop to recursion (10 marks)
questions.prompt: Convert the method `static int sumStep(int n) { int s = 0; for (int i = n; i > 0; i = i - 2) { s += i; } return s; }` to a recursive method with two parameters, and trace both for `n = 9`. (10 marks)

steps.title: Apply the rules
steps.body: The loop changes `i` and `s`, so both become parameters. The base case is the opposite of `i > 0`, which is `i <= 0`, and it returns `s`. The body and the update become the call `sumStepRec(i - 2, s + i)`. The first call is `sumStepRec(n, 0)`. (4 marks)

steps.title: The method
steps.body: `static int sumStepRec(int i, int s) { if (i <= 0) { return s; } return sumStepRec(i - 2, s + i); }`. (3 marks)

steps.title: Trace for 9
steps.body: `(9, 0)`, `(7, 9)`, `(5, 16)`, `(3, 21)`, `(1, 24)`, then `(-1, 25)` where `i <= 0` is true and the method returns 25. The loop adds 9, 7, 5, 3 and 1 to reach 25. (3 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** Both versions return **25** for `n = 9`; the base case is a range because `i` steps by 2 and can jump from 1 to -1.

questions.title: Question 9: Backtracking and Towers of Hanoi (10 marks)
questions.prompt: (a) The method `subsets(a, i, chosen)` takes `a[i]`, calls itself with `i + 1`, removes `a[i]` again, and calls itself with `i + 1` once more, stopping when `i == a.length`. State the number of calls for an array of 3 elements and give the formula for n elements. (b) State the number of moves needed to carry 4 disks in Towers of Hanoi and give the recurrence. (c) Why is the removal in (a) needed? (10 marks)

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: Each call at depth `d` makes two calls at depth `d + 1`, down to depth n, so the calls are 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = **15** for n = 3. In general the sum is 2 to the (n + 1) minus 1. (4 marks)

steps.title: Part (b)
steps.body: `moves(n) = 2 * moves(n - 1) + 1` with `moves(0) = 0`, which is 2 to the n minus 1. For 4 disks the moves are 1, 3, 7, **15**. (3 marks)

steps.title: Part (c)
steps.body: The list `chosen` is shared by every branch. Without the removal the element stays in the list when the second call starts, so every later subset also contains it and the lists printed are wrong and growing. The removal restores the state before the next choice. (3 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answers.** (a) 15 calls, 2 to the (n + 1) minus 1; (b) 15 moves; (c) the undo restores the shared state.

questions.title: Question 10: Calls and depth (8 marks)
questions.prompt: A method `sumLinear(lo, hi)` adds the numbers from `lo` to `hi` one at a time, and `sumHalves(a, lo, hi)` adds the elements of an array by splitting the range in half until one element remains. For 16 elements, state the number of calls and the greatest depth of the stack of each (the first call is depth 1), and say which is more likely to overflow the stack for a very large input. (8 marks)

steps.title: Linear
steps.body: One call for each of the 16 numbers plus one for the empty range: **17 calls**, and each is one level deeper than the last, so the greatest depth is **17**. (3 marks)

steps.title: Halving
steps.body: One call per element and one for each split above them: 2n - 1 = **31 calls**. The range is halved 4 times (16, 8, 4, 2, 1), so the greatest depth is **5**. (3 marks)

steps.title: Overflow
steps.body: The linear version, because its depth grows with n; the halving version needs only about log2 n frames even though it makes more calls in total. (2 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** Linear: 17 calls, depth 17. Halving: 31 calls, depth 5. The linear version is more likely to overflow the stack.
